claim: The chromosomal replication origin region (ori) of characterised bacteria is dynamically positioned throughout the cell cycle.
source: The chromosomal replication origin region (ori) of characterised bacteria is dynamically positioned throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: This is a general statement about bacterial ori positioning that is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: In slowly growing Escherichia coli, ori is maintained at mid-cell from birth until its replication.
source: In slowly growing Escherichia coli, ori is maintained at mid-cell from birth until its replication, after which newly replicated sister oris move to opposite quarter positions.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about ori positioning in E. coli and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: After replication, newly replicated sister oris move to opposite quarter positions in slowly growing E. coli.
source: In slowly growing Escherichia coli, ori is maintained at mid-cell from birth until its replication, after which newly replicated sister oris move to opposite quarter positions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: MukBEF forms dynamically positioned clusters on the chromosome.
source: We provide an explanation for ori positioning based on the self-organisation of the Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes complex, MukBEF, which forms dynamically positioned clusters on the chromosome.
evidence: This is stated as a property of MukBEF and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A non-trivial feedback between the self-organising gradient of MukBEF complexes and the oris leads to accurate ori positioning.
source: We propose that a non-trivial feedback between the self-organising gradient of MukBEF complexes and the oris leads to accurate ori positioning.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors and is tested through computational modeling and experimental validation.

claim: The model finds excellent agreement with quantitative experimental measurements.
source: We find excellent agreement with quantitative experimental measurements and confirm key predictions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Oris exhibit biased motion towards MukBEF clusters, rather than mid-cell.
source: Specifically, we show that oris exhibit biased motion towards MukBEF clusters, rather than mid-cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1d and supported by the velocity profile analysis.

claim: MukBEF and oris act together as a self-organising system in chromosome organisation-segregation.
source: Our findings suggest that MukBEF and oris act together as a self-organising system in chromosome organisation-segregation and introduces protein self-organisation as an important consideration for future studies of chromosome dynamics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In new-born E. coli cells growing under relatively slow growing conditions, the 'home' position of the origin is at mid-cell.
source: In new-born Escherichia coli cells growing under relatively slow growing conditions in which initiation of replication and its completion occur within a single cell generation, the 'home' position of the origin (henceforth and in the model, ori) is at mid-cell (Nielsen et al., 2006b; Niki et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by three citations to previous experimental work.

claim: After replication, duplicated origins experience 10–15 min of 'cohesion' arising at least in part from interlinking of the two daughter chromosomes (precatenation).
source: After replication, and consequent 10–15 min of 'cohesion', arising at least in part from interlinking of the two daughter chromosomes (precatenation) (Joshi et al., 2011; Nicolas et al., 2014; Nielsen et al., 2006a; Nolivos et al., 2016; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008), duplicated origins migrate rapidly to opposite quarter positions, which become the new home positions for the remainder of the cell cycle (Cass et al., 2016; Kuwada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Duplicated origins migrate rapidly to opposite quarter positions after cohesion.
source: After replication, and consequent 10–15 min of 'cohesion', arising at least in part from interlinking of the two daughter chromosomes (precatenation) (Joshi et al., 2011; Nicolas et al., 2014; Nielsen et al., 2006a; Nolivos et al., 2016; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008), duplicated origins migrate rapidly to opposite quarter positions, which become the new home positions for the remainder of the cell cycle (Cass et al., 2016; Kuwada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: E. coli and its relatives do not carry ParABS systems that facilitate the segregation of low copy plasmids and some other bacterial chromosomes.
source: This is particularly the case in E. coli and its relatives, which do not carry ParABS systems that facilitate the segregation of low copy plasmids and some other bacterial chromosomes (Livny et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: MukBEF is a functional homolog of ubiquitous Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complexes.
source: However, MukBEF, a functional homolog of ubiquitous Structural Maintenance of Chromosomes (SMC) complexes (Nolivos and Sherratt, 2014; Rybenkov et al., 2014), plays a role in E. coli chromosome organisation-segregation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: MukBEF recruits the type II topoisomerase Topo IV.
source: One of its functions is to recruit the type II topoisomerase Topo IV (Li et al., 2010; Nicolas et al., 2014), which is required for the timely removal of catenanes from newly replicated sister chromosomes (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Topo IV is required for the timely removal of catenanes from newly replicated sister chromosomes.
source: One of its functions is to recruit the type II topoisomerase Topo IV (Li et al., 2010; Nicolas et al., 2014), which is required for the timely removal of catenanes from newly replicated sister chromosomes (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Under slow growth conditions, MukBEF forms a small number of dynamic clusters located at the middle or quarter positions.
source: Under slow growth conditions, MukBEF forms a small number of dynamic clusters (visualised as fluorescent foci) located at the middle or quarter positions (den Blaauwen et al., 2001; Ohsumi et al., 2001), in close association with ori (Danilova et al., 2007), and the splitting and movement of these foci occurs concurrently with the segregation of oris to the quarter positions (Danilova et al., 2007; Nicolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MukBEF clusters are in close association with ori.
source: Under slow growth conditions, MukBEF forms a small number of dynamic clusters (visualised as fluorescent foci) located at the middle or quarter positions (den Blaauwen et al., 2001; Ohsumi et al., 2001), in close association with ori (Danilova et al., 2007), and the splitting and movement of these foci occurs concurrently with the segregation of oris to the quarter positions (Danilova et al., 2007; Nicolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The splitting and movement of MukBEF foci occurs concurrently with the segregation of oris to the quarter positions.
source: Under slow growth conditions, MukBEF forms a small number of dynamic clusters (visualised as fluorescent foci) located at the middle or quarter positions (den Blaauwen et al., 2001; Ohsumi et al., 2001), in close association with ori (Danilova et al., 2007), and the splitting and movement of these foci occurs concurrently with the segregation of oris to the quarter positions (Danilova et al., 2007; Nicolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MukBEF foci consist of on average 16 dimeric slowly-diffusing MukBEF complexes.
source: Foci consist of on average 16 dimeric slowly-diffusing MukBEF complexes (Badrinarayanan et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The colocalisation of MukBEF with ori is not required for either MukBEF foci formation or positioning.
source: The colocalisation with ori is not required for either MukBEF foci formation or positioning: depletion of Topo IV results in cells with multiple catenated oris forming a single focus at mid-cell but with multiple MukBEF clusters positioned throughout the nucleoid (Nicolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: MukBEF clusters are not necessarily assembled at or bound to ori.
source: Thus MukBEF clusters are not necessarily assembled at or bound to ori, consistent with the lack of any sequence specificity (Nolivos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from experimental observations and supported by a citation.

claim: MukBEF binds DNA non-specifically.
source: Thus MukBEF clusters are not necessarily assembled at or bound to ori, consistent with the lack of any sequence specificity (Nolivos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Restoration of Topo IV activity leads to the decatenated oris moving to the MukBEF clusters.
source: Furthermore, restoration of Topo IV activity leads to the decatenated oris moving to the MukBEF clusters suggesting that MukBEF recruits or positions ori (Nicolas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Depletion of functional MukBEF results in ori mis-positioning that is subsequently restored upon repletion.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, depletion of functional MukBEF results in ori mis-positioning that is subsequently restored upon repletion (Badrinarayanan et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Molecules in MukBEF clusters turnover continuously with a timescale of about one minute.
source: Given that molecules in the clusters turnover continuously with a timescale of about one minute (Badrinarayanan et al., 2012b) and that MukBEF binds DNA non-specifically, how does it even form clusters?
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: A stochastic Turing pattern can explain the positioning of MukBEF clusters.
source: We have proposed that a self-positioning stochastic Turing pattern can explain the positioning of MukBEF clusters (Murray and Sourjik, 2017) (see the methods section for a review).
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: A Turing pattern is a spatial pattern in the concentration of a reactant in a reaction-diffusion system that arises spontaneously due to a diffusion-driven instability.
source: A Turing pattern is a spatial pattern in the concentration of a reactant in a reaction-diffusion system that arises spontaneously due to a diffusion-driven instability (Koch and Meinhardt, 1994; Turing, 1952).
evidence: This is a definition of a Turing pattern supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: A flux-balance mechanism and stochasticity work together to ensure that a specific Turing pattern is selected in the MukBEF system.
source: We used the Turing mechanism to explain the positioning of MukBEF foci and showed that a flux-balance mechanism and stochasticity work together to ensure that a specific Turing pattern is selected: short cells consistently have a single centre-positioned peak in the MukBEF concentration, while longer cells have quarter positioned peaks.
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work and its findings.

claim: Short cells consistently have a single centre-positioned peak in the MukBEF concentration.
source: We used the Turing mechanism to explain the positioning of MukBEF foci and showed that a flux-balance mechanism and stochasticity work together to ensure that a specific Turing pattern is selected: short cells consistently have a single centre-positioned peak in the MukBEF concentration, while longer cells have quarter positioned peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Longer cells have quarter positioned MukBEF peaks.
source: We used the Turing mechanism to explain the positioning of MukBEF foci and showed that a flux-balance mechanism and stochasticity work together to ensure that a specific Turing pattern is selected: short cells consistently have a single centre-positioned peak in the MukBEF concentration, while longer cells have quarter positioned peaks.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: MukBEF requires energy in the form of ATP to establish a self-organised gradient.
source: MukBEF requires energy in the form of ATP to establish a self-organised gradient but it is not pulled to the middle or quarter positions by any active force.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the model and is consistent with known biochemical properties of MukBEF.

claim: MukBEF is not pulled to the middle or quarter positions by any active force.
source: MukBEF requires energy in the form of ATP to establish a self-organised gradient but it is not pulled to the middle or quarter positions by any active force.
evidence: This is a key feature of the self-organization model proposed by the authors.

claim: The attraction of ori up the MukBEF gradient may be due to energetic considerations and the elastic nature of the chromosome resulting in an effective force and directed motion.
source: Similarly, the attraction of ori up the MukBEF gradient may be due to energetic considerations and the elastic nature of the chromosome (a DNA-relay) resulting on the macro scale in an effective (rectification) force and directed motion.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism that is later tested using polymer simulations.

claim: MukBEF foci and ori are much more colocalised than would be expected if they were positioned independently.
source: When we did this, we found that MukBEF foci and ori are much more colocalised than would be expected if they were positioned independently (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing measured and expected distributions in Figure 1c.

claim: There is a relatively strong positive correlation (r = 0.8) between MukBEF and ori positions.
source: This was confirmed by the relatively strong positive correlation (r = 0.8) between MukBEF and ori positions (using a robust correlation based on the median absolute deviation [Shevlyakov, 1997]).
evidence: This is a statistical measure calculated from the experimental data.

claim: Ori experiences a greater restoring velocity towards the MukBEF focus than towards mid-cell.
source: Comparing these two profiles, we found that ori experiences a greater restoring velocity towards the MukBEF focus than towards mid-cell (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the velocity profile analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Ori is not attracted to mid-cell per se, rather it is more likely attracted to the MukBEF focus, which happens to be positioned at mid-cell.
source: This indicates that ori is not attracted to mid-cell per se, rather it is more likely attracted to the MukBEF focus, which happens to be positioned at mid-cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the velocity profile data in Figure 1d.

claim: MukBEF positions ori in E. coli.
source: Hence, together with previous results, these data strongly indicate that MukBEF positions ori in E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous work.

claim: MukBEF foci display similar biases towards ori and mid-cell.
source: When we examined the restoring velocity of MukBEF foci, we found that they displayed similar biases towards ori and mid-cell (Figure 1e), suggesting that MukBEF foci are equally attracted to mid-cell and ori and that therefore the attraction between MukBEF and ori may be indeed be bi-directional.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the velocity profile analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The attraction between MukBEF and ori may be bi-directional.
source: When we examined the restoring velocity of MukBEF foci, we found that they displayed similar biases towards ori and mid-cell (Figure 1e), suggesting that MukBEF foci are equally attracted to mid-cell and ori and that therefore the attraction between MukBEF and ori may be indeed be bi-directional.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the velocity profile data in Figure 1e.

claim: Co-localisation with MukBEF is strongest for ori and becomes progressively weaker for ori-distant loci.
source: This is supported by the observation that co-localisation with MukBEF is strongest for ori and becomes progressively weaker for ori-distant loci (Danilova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: MukBEF is preferentially loaded onto the chromosome within the ori region.
source: In particular, we propose that MukBEF is preferentially loaded onto the chromosome within the ori region.
evidence: This is the key hypothesis proposed by the authors for their model.

claim: SMC is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites by the protein ParB in Bacillus subtilis and other bacteria.
source: This is the case for SMC, a distant relative of MukBEF (see Gruber, 2018 for a review). In Bacillus subtilis and other bacteria SMC is loaded onto the chromosome at parS sites by the protein ParB.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: No analogue of ParB/parS has yet been discovered in E. coli.
source: While no analogue of ParB/parS has yet been discovered in E. coli, in the following we will focus on exploring the effect of preferential loading and examining whether it gives results that are consistent with experimental observations.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about E. coli.

claim: Ori tracks the self-organised MukBEF focus, resulting in mid-cell positioning in simulations of short cells.
source: We found, as expected, that ori tracks the self-organised MukBEF focus, resulting in mid-cell positioning (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The model reproduces a linear velocity profile for ori similar to experimental observations.
source: Given the self-organising and fluctuating nature of the MukBEF gradient in our model (which is representative of the in vivo behaviour), it was not obvious that the model would reproduce the observed relationship. However, we indeed found a similarly linear velocity profile.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing simulation results with experimental data.

claim: By adjusting only two parameters (ori diffusion constant and drift parameter), the model obtains good agreement with experimental values for apparent diffusion constant and drift rate.
source: We found that by adjusting only two parameters, the ori diffusion constant and drift parameter, we were able to obtain good agreement with the values obtained from the experimental data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fitting results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claim: At 0.2 µm from mid-cell, the restoring force on ori is 0.02 pN.
source: At 0.2 µm from mid-cell this gives a restoring force of 0.02 pN, similar to the value measured in an in vitro reconstitution of a plasmid partitioning ParABS system (Vecchiarelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is calculated from the model parameters and compared to experimental measurements from another system.

claim: Preferential loading of MukBEF at a fixed spatial location perturbs the positioning of the self-organised MukBEF foci due to the modified flux differential across foci.
source: In previous work, we showed that preferential loading at a fixed spatial location perturbs the positioning of the self-organised MukBEF foci due to the modified flux differential across foci (Murray and Sourjik, 2017).
evidence: This is a reference to the authors' previous work.

claim: Preferential loading has a suppressive effect on noise in ori and MukBEF positioning at intermediate levels.
source: This was observed to have a suppressive effect on noise (Figure 2—figure supplement 4a). At intermediate levels of preferential loading, the positions of both MukBEF and ori deviate less from mid-cell.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Preferential loading results in stronger colocalisation of ori with the MukBEF focus.
source: We also found that preferential loading resulted in stronger colocalisation of ori with the MukBEF focus and this led to excellent agreement with previous measurements of their separation distance (Figure 2—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4b.

claim: An intermediate level of preferential loading (6x) appears to be most consistent with experimental observations.
source: Thus, an intermediate level of preferential loading appears to be most consistent with experimental observations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulation results at different preferential loading ratios with experimental data.

claim: With 6x preferential loading, the model shows excellent agreement with experimental ori position distributions and velocity profiles.
source: We were able to find new values for the diffusion and drift parameters that lead to excellent agreement with the experimental values (Figure 2f). Furthermore, the resulting distribution of the ori positions showed better agreement with the experimental distribution, with the fat tails observed in the absence of preferential loading no longer present (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of simulation and experimental results in Figure 2e,f.

claim: Without preferential loading, approximately half of the simulations have both oris near the same quarter position.
source: However, we found that without preferential loading approximately half of the individual simulations have both oris near the same quarter position (Figure 3a), clearly indicating that partitioning was not accurate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A model of ori simply moving up the MukBEF gradient is not sufficient to explain partitioning.
source: Evidently, a model of ori simply moving up the MukBEF gradient is not sufficient to explain partitioning as the noise inherent to the system means that it can switch stochastically between partitioned and un-partitioned states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results without preferential loading.

claim: Preferential loading results in stable and accurate partitioning of ori.
source: However we found that preferential loading resulted in stable and accurate partitioning (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A preferential loading ratio greater than six is sufficient to ensure that one and only one ori is positioned to each quarter position and they do not interchange.
source: A preferential loading ratio greater than six (i.e. six times more loading than elsewhere) was sufficient to ensure that one and only one ori was positioned to each quarter position and they do not interchange (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Preferential loading changes the stability of the different steady states of the system.
source: These results demonstrate that preferential loading of MukBEF changes the stability of the different steady states of the system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results comparing different preferential loading ratios.

claim: Without preferential loading during growth, duplicated oris often remain associated to the same MukBEF focus, resulting in a partitioning accuracy of only 25% by the end of the cell cycle.
source: We first examined growth in the absence of preferential loading. Similarly to what we observed previously in the simulations of non-growing cells (Figure 3a), we found that duplicated oris often remained associated to the same MukBEF focus, resulting in a partitioning accuracy (defined as before as the fraction of simulations with oris in opposite cell halves) of only 25% by the end of the cell cycle (120 min) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Preferential loading delays the splitting of MukBEF foci during growth.
source: When we introduced preferential loading at ori, we found firstly that it delayed the splitting of MukBEF foci, similar to a spatially fixed loading site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d) (Murray and Sourjik, 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: In experimental observations, approximately 95% of cells have partitioned ori already 20 min after initial separation, with oris being separated at that point by an average distance of 33% of the cell length.
source: Clearly, this level of partitioning accuracy is not representative of the biological situation, where ~ 95% of cells have partitioned ori already 20 min after initial separation, with oris being separated at that point by an average distance of 33% of the cell length.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation that the model needs to reproduce.

claim: Newly replicated oris experience entropic repulsion of two closed loops.
source: In particular, newly replicated oris would experience the entropic repulsion of two closed loops.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about polymer physics and chromosome organization.

claim: Duplicated oris experience an initially large segregation velocity.
source: This is consistent with experimental observations, in which duplicated oris (and indeed all loci) experience an initially large segregation velocity (Cass et al., 2016; Lampo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: The effective potential associated with entropic repulsion has the approximate form of a (half) Gaussian in the centre-of-mass separation.
source: Numerical studies have demonstrated that the effective potential associated with such a repulsion has the approximate form of a (half) Gaussian in the centre-of-mass separation (Bohn and Heermann, 2011; Bohn and Heermann, 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous numerical studies.

claim: Entropic repulsion on its own (without preferential loading) is not able to reproduce the observed partitioning behavior.
source: We found that entropic repulsion on its own (i.e. no preferential loading) was not able to reproduce the observed behaviour.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter sweep results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combining preferential loading with short-range entropic repulsion of ori gives much closer agreement with measured partitioning accuracy and relative separation.
source: On the other hand, combining preferential loading with short-range entropic repulsion of ori, gave the properties of both and allowed the model output to move much closer to the measured partitioning accuracy and relative separation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and resulted in kymographs with the experimentally observed behaviours (Figure 4a–d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Short-range entropic repulsion destabilises the undesirable configuration (both oris at same MukBEF peak) so that system switches to the quarter positioned configuration.
source: The short-range entropic repulsion destabilises the undesirable configuration so that system switches, in a timely manner, to the quarter positioned configuration.
evidence: This is an explanation of the mechanism by which the model achieves accurate partitioning.

claim: The model with preferential loading and entropic repulsion shows good agreement with experimental segregation velocity and partitioning accuracy time-courses.
source: We found good agreement between two cell length independent measures: the segregation velocity (the change of the absolute distance between oris between time points) and the partitioning accuracy (Figure 4e,f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of simulation and experimental results in Figure 4e,f.

claim: With the addition of entropic repulsion, the model is capable of reproducing the observed ori dynamics in growing cells.
source: Thus, with the addition of entropic repulsion, the model is capable of reproducing the observed ori dynamics in growing cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of simulation and experimental results.

claim: The elastic nature of the chromosome can be harnessed to power directed motion of partitioning complexes.
source: It has previously been argued in the DNA relay and Brownian ratchet models of partition complex positioning by the ParABS system (Hu et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2014; Surovtsev et al., 2016) that the elastic nature of the chromosome itself (Wiggins et al., 2010) can be harnessed to power directed motion of partitioning complexes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work on ParABS systems.

claim: MukBEF promotes long-range DNA interactions in vivo.
source: It has recently been demonstrated in vivo that MukBEF promotes long-range DNA interactions (Lioy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent experimental work.

claim: A spatially dependent looping probability along the long axis of the nucleoid representing the MukBEF concentration profile results in ori being positioned to the middle of the nucleoid.
source: We found that this resulted in the ori being positioned to the middle of the nucleoid, where the looping probability was greatest (Figure 5b, blue line).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The positioning of ori affects the organisation of the entire polymer, which takes up a left-ori/ter-right configuration.
source: We also found that the positioning of ori affected the organisation of the entire polymer, which took with up a left-ori/ter-right configuration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous results on the effect of a forced localisation of ori (Junier et al., 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous work.

claim: Ori experiences a restoring velocity towards mid-cell in polymer simulations with spatially-varying looping probability.
source: When we examined the velocity of the ori as a function of the long-axis position, we found that the ori indeed experiences a restoring velocity towards mid-cell i.e. directed movement (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Elastic fluctuations of the polymer power the movement of ori up the gradient in the looping probability.
source: In this way, elastic fluctuations of the polymer power the movement of ori up the gradient in the looping probability.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the polymer simulation results.

claim: Directed movement of ori up the MukBEF gradient can plausibly arise due to a MukBEF-mediated, spatially-varying looping probability.
source: Thus, directed movement of ori up the MukBEF gradient can plausibly arise due to a MukBEF-mediated, spatially-varying looping probability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the polymer simulation results.

claim: Looping has a positive effect on ori segregation in polymer simulations with two chromosomes.
source: Indeed, we found this to be the case. Looping had a positive effect on ori segregation (Figure 5d): the greater the looping, the faster ori were segregated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Oris are positioned by the spatially varying looping probability to opposite quarter positions along the long axis of the cell in polymer simulations.
source: Furthermore, the ori are not just segregated but are positioned by the spatially varying looping probability to opposite quarter positions along the long axis of the cell in the same way as for the single chromosome case (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Oris experience an effective restoring force around their respective quarter positions in polymer simulations.
source: Similarly, we found that the oris experience an effective restoring force around their respective quarter positions (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the polymer simulation results shown in Figure 5f.

claim: A spatially-varying probability for ori to form loops with other DNA leads to directed movement of oris to the locations of MukBEF foci and can accelerate ori segregation.
source: Overall, these results indicate that a spatially-varying probability for ori to forms loops with other DNA (nominally due to the localised action of MukBEF) leads, in the manner of a DNA relay, to directed movement of oris to the locations where the probability is greatest, i.e. to the locations of MukBEF foci and, furthermore, that this can accelerate ori segregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the polymer simulation results.

claim: A self-organising MukBEF gradient can accurately reproduce the observed ori dynamics, apparent diffusion constant and drift rate.
source: We find that a self-organising MukBEF gradient can indeed accurately reproduce the observed ori dynamics, apparent diffusion constant and drift rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the stochastic simulations.

claim: Preferential loading of MukBEF within ori introduces a non-trivial interaction between MukBEF foci and oris that leads to accurate and stable partitioning as an emergent property of the system.
source: A proposed preferential loading of MukBEF within ori introduces a non-trivial interaction between MukBEF foci and oris that leads to accurate and stable partitioning as an emergent property of the system.
evidence: This is a summary of the main mechanism proposed by the model.

claim: The model does not contain any actual directed force on MukBEF or ori.
source: Importantly, the model does not contain any actual directed force.
evidence: This is a key feature of the self-organization model.

claim: Preferential loading stabilises the desirable quarter-positioned configuration, preventing stochastic switching to the undesirable configuration.
source: Preferential loading stabilises the desirable quarter-positioned configuration, preventing stochastic switching to the undesirable configuration having both oris associated to the same MukBEF focus (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism by which preferential loading ensures accurate partitioning.

claim: The model predicts that whatever the nature of the MukBEF-ori relationship, it leads to an effective mutual attraction between ori and MukBEF foci.
source: Therefore, the fundamental prediction of our model is not necessarily that MukBEF is loaded at sites within the ori region, as for SMC, but rather that whatever the nature of the MukBEF-ori relationship, it is such that it leads to an effective mutual attraction between ori and MukBEF foci.
evidence: This is stated as the fundamental prediction of the model.

claim: The specificity of ori must be specified, directly or indirectly, by some sequence (or sequences) within the ori region.
source: In any case, the specificity of ori must be specified, directly or indirectly, by some sequence (or sequences) within the ori region.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how ori specificity must be encoded.

claim: The actual site of replication initiation, oriC, is not responsible for ori positioning because moving it to another location on the chromosome does not affect ori positioning.
source: We know that the actual site of replication initiation, oriC, is not responsible because moving it to another location on the chromosome does not affect ori positioning (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous experimental work.

claim: If the unknown 'centromeric' sequence were inserted into a plasmid lacking a partitioning system, the resulting plasmids would colocalise with MukBEF foci and be maintained in the absence of their own partitioning system.
source: If this unknown 'centromeric' sequence were inserted into a plasmid lacking a partitioning system, then we would predict that the resulting plasmids would colocalise with MukBEF foci just like the ori, and thereby be maintained in the absence of their own partitioning system.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the authors based on their model.

claim: The model can recapitulate ori positioning during faster growth with multiple replication forks when taking into account the higher copy number of MukBEF.
source: Taking into account the higher copy number of MukBEF in faster growing cells (Li et al., 2014), we found very consistent ori dynamics (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: During faster growth, ori and MukBEF remain in tight association and MukBEF splitting is coincident with ori separation.
source: Similar to the slow growth case, we observed that ori and MukBEF remain in tight association and MukBEF splitting is coincident with ori separation, so that there are approximately as many MukBEF foci as ori.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results for faster growth conditions.

claim: 95% of ori foci are within the centre 44% of the cell width, corresponding to a region 0.33 µm wide.
source: 95% of ori foci are within the centre 44% of the cell width, corresponding to a region 0.33 µm wide.
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: 95% of MukB-mYPet foci are within the centre 39% of the cell width, corresponding to a region 0.30 µm wide.
source: 95% of MukB-mYPet foci are within the centre 39% of the cell width, corresponding to a region 0.30 µm wide.
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Both ori and MukB are confined within the transverse direction to the centre region of the cell.
source: This is justified as both ori and MukB are confined within the transverse direction to the centre region of the cell: 95% of foci are within the centre 40% (300 nm) of the cell width (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d–g).
evidence: This is measured from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d-g.

claim: The arc length from MukBEF's hinge domain to either of its two head domains is about 70 nm.
source: MukBEF is also a very large molecule complex, with the arc length from its hinge domain to either of its two head domains being about 70 nm (Matoba et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural work.

claim: Cells were treated with DL serine hydroxamate (SHX) to enrich for cells with a single ori focus.
source: To enrich for such cells, we treated a strain carrying fluorescently labelled MukB and ori (Figure 1a) with DL serine hydroxamate (SHX).
evidence: This is described in the methods section as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: DL serine hydroxamate triggers the stringent response thereby inhibiting DNA replication initiation.
source: This structural analogue of serine triggers the stringent response thereby inhibiting DNA replication initiation (Ferullo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

source: Cells have a mean length of 2.2 µm.
